questions.heading: The overall aesthetic
questions.ask: Which overall aesthetic should Wargrid pursue, rather than replacing the original primitive graphics with traditional pixel sprites?
questions.selected: High-contrast flat geometric abstraction inspired by Space Invaders; the contrast from the early C image is valuable, but its faux-detailed/pixel-art look is not.
questions.exact_user: You said we should not replace them with pixel art, but above all three are pixel art. I was thinking more about space invaders and rectangles, circles and triangles. That being said what I like about your screenshot C is the high contrast. It dies go in the right direction
options: Precision diagram — crisp, flat, abstract and functional.
Geometric diorama — chunky shapes, subtle depth, tactile and playful.
Neon tactical — dark, futuristic, glowy and digital.
B + A readability + selective C effects (the assistant’s *initial* preference, superseded).
questions.rationale: The user challenged the initial image direction: all three felt too much like pixel/low-poly art. The revised north star is deliberately primitive rectangles, circles, triangles and lines. Keep C’s high contrast, not its visual complexity.
images: Original A/B/C concept triptych (unaltered generated image)

questions.heading: How abstract should the units be?
questions.ask: How should simple rectangles, circles, triangles and lines convey recognizable roles?
questions.selected: B — Functional icons made from simple primitives.
questions.exact_user: For Wargrid art direction question 2, I choose B: functional icons made from simple primitives. Continue the interview.
options: Pure symbols — as few components as possible, almost arcade-like.
Functional icons — recognizable tracks, turrets, blades and machinery from simple primitives.
Adaptive abstraction — pure symbols at far zoom; functional icons at normal gameplay zoom.
questions.rationale: Role clarity matters more than decorative fidelity. At normal gameplay zoom a tank must read as a tank, and a bulldozer as a bulldozer, without labels.
images: Revised flat geometric battlefield (unaltered generated image)

questions.heading: Filled shapes or outlines?
questions.ask: How should geometric primitives be rendered?
questions.selected: C — Hybrid filled geometric shapes with selective outlines and accents.
questions.exact_user: For Wargrid art direction question 3, I choose C — Hybrid filled geometric shapes with selective outlines and accents. Continue the interview.
options: Solid shapes — bold filled forms, strongly reminiscent of classic arcade graphics.
Outlines — wireframe-like tactical display, highly abstract.
Hybrid — filled shapes with selected outlines, highlights and contrasting accents.
questions.rationale: Mass is conveyed by fills; an outline is added only where it clarifies depth, silhouette, selection or meaning.

questions.heading: How much personality should the geometry have?
questions.ask: How much mechanical motion and exaggeration should accompany each action?
questions.exact_user: For Wargrid art direction question 4, I choose B — Responsive and punchy animations. Continue the interview.
options: Mechanical and restrained — rigid, realistic rotation and recoil.
Responsive and punchy — recoil, small hull reactions, impacts, debris and bursts.
Exaggerated arcade — bounce, squash/stretch, huge reactions.
Mechanical units, exaggerated effects — unchosen option.
questions.rationale: Movement and impact should be felt without turning large-scale combat into a bouncy cartoon.
questions.extra: Between questions 4 and 5, the user additionally said: “The game should still be isometric, so i guess at some point they will have to look a bit 3d. Or could it work flat? I suppose that will look strange”. This led directly to Question 5.

questions.heading: How much depth should our shapes have?
questions.ask: How should flat primitives communicate physical depth within the existing isometric perspective?
questions.selected: B — Minimalist 2.5D with simple top and side faces.
questions.exact_user: For Wargrid art direction question 5, I choose B — Minimalist 2.5D with simple top and side faces. Continue the interview.
options: Flat symbols — objects could resemble board markers painted on terrain.
Minimalist 2.5D — a top and one/two darker side faces, no elaborate 3D art.
Detailed geometric 3D — additional surfaces, mechanical details, more realistic depth.
Flat infantry with 2.5D vehicles and buildings — unchosen option.
questions.rationale: Use cheap, deliberate extrusion to give objects presence, not conventional 3D meshes or textured sprites.

questions.heading: What should the terrain look like?
questions.ask: What should the battlefield do visually while still identifying different maps?
questions.selected: C — Muted biomes with bright units and effects.
questions.exact_user: For Wargrid art direction question 6, I choose C — Muted biomes with bright units and effects. Continue the interview.
options: Tactical board — near-black terrain, subtle grid, abstract command display.
Colored biomes — saturated sand, greenery, snow and other natural colors.
Muted biomes — recognizable but desaturated/darker desert, forest, snow etc.
Mostly tactical board with distinct geometric environmental features — unchosen option.
questions.rationale: Terrain should have location identity without stealing contrast from player colors or combat effects. Prominent full-map grids are unnecessary.

questions.heading: What should combat effects look like?
questions.ask: How much geometry, fragmentation, smoke, glow and spectacle belong in explosions?
questions.selected: D — Hybrid: geometric destruction for normal combat and cinematic geometric effects for powerful attacks.
questions.exact_user: For Wargrid art direction question 7, I choose D — Hybrid: geometric destruction for normal combat and cinematic geometric effects for powerful attacks. Continue the interview.
options: Tactical — expanding circles, lines and small precise flashes.
Geometric destruction — angular bright polygons, chunks of debris, simple smoke.
Geometric spectacle — large shockwaves, powerful flashes, glow and layered particles.
B for ordinary combat, C only for particularly powerful attacks (chosen hybrid).
questions.rationale: Everyday fighting stays legible and relatively inexpensive; superweapons and major events may briefly be spectacular. Scale down redundant particles during heavy battles.

questions.heading: Should each faction have its own geometric language?
questions.ask: How should USA, China and FRC be identifiable while using the same geometric primitives?
questions.exact_user: For Wargrid art direction question 8, I choose B — Shared functions, faction-specific styling. Continue the interview.
options: Shared geometry with different colors — economical, limited faction identity.
Shared function silhouettes, different construction styles and proportions.
Completely distinct shape languages for each faction — recognizable but may hurt role readability.
Mostly B with radical differentiation for iconic objects — unchosen option.
questions.rationale: Role → faction → owner: a tank reads as tank first, as USA/China/FRC second, then shows player color independently. The illustrative faction colors are examples, not mandated ownership colors.

questions.heading: How should buildings communicate their purpose?
questions.ask: Can a power plant and a war factory be recognizable from physical structure alone?
questions.selected: D — Functional building silhouettes with selective mechanical animations.
questions.exact_user: For Wargrid art direction question 9, I choose D — Functional building silhouettes with selective mechanical animations. Continue the interview.
options: Symbolic buildings — box-shaped structures differentiated mainly with icons.
Functional silhouettes — distinct power-generator structures, factory doors, supply areas and so on.
B + selective C: strong functional silhouette, purposeful animations (chosen hybrid).
questions.rationale: A factory should be recognizable in a still, then become lively when its door opens. A plant should have identifiable generators, then pulse when active.
questions.special: The original illustration compared a **power plant and war factory**, not separate A/B/C/D artwork. Only those two original object illustrations exist.

questions.heading: Lighting, shadows and glow
questions.ask: Should units feel like physical matte objects or luminous tactical holograms?
questions.selected: D — Matte and shaded objects with selective luminous components and effects.
questions.exact_user: For Wargrid art direction question 10, I choose D — Matte and shaded objects with selective luminous components and effects. Continue the interview.
options: Pure graphic contrast — virtually no lighting and shadows.
Matte/shaded geometry — brighter tops, darker sides, shadows, minor highlights.
Luminous geometry — always-glowing outlines, rim lights and accents.
B with selective C — energy components, shots, selection and important effects glow.
questions.rationale: Do not glow every hull edge; reserve strong luminance for communication and emphasis.

questions.heading: How should detail change when zooming out?
questions.ask: How do hundreds of units remain recognizable at smaller on-screen sizes?
questions.exact_user: For Wargrid art direction question 11, I choose B — Progressive simplification. Continue the interview.
options: Consistent geometry — same drawing at every zoom; detail simply disappears.
Progressive simplification — remove accents while preserving hull, turret, barrel, blade etc.
Tactical icon transition — switch to strategic icons at far zoom.
B plus optional separate tactical overview mode — unchosen option.
questions.rationale: Role-defining structures are sacred. Outlines, minor highlights and tiny moving pieces are expendable; effects also scale with crowding.

questions.heading: How much player color should units have?
questions.ask: What portion of visible surfaces should show the owner color rather than neutral materials?
questions.selected: B — Balanced player-colored surfaces with neutral sides.
questions.exact_user: For Wargrid art direction question 12, I choose B — Balanced player-colored surfaces with neutral sides. Continue the interview.
options: Full color — most of each unit uses the owner’s color.
Balanced — strong owner color on large upper-facing surfaces, darker neutral sides/machinery.
Color accents — neutral charcoal/steel machinery with small owner-color details.
B, but infantry and very small units with more ownership color — unchosen option.
questions.rationale: Top-facing faction/ownership surfaces must be readable from the camera; avoid hiding color in thin edge strokes.

questions.heading: How polished should the simplicity feel?
questions.ask: Should Wargrid be raw arcade minimalism, refined primitives or high-production geometric spectacle?
questions.exact_user: For Wargrid art direction question 13, I choose B — Refined geometric minimalism. Please now create the complete AI-ready Wargrid art direction Markdown document and visual reference package based on our 13 decisions, with concrete Godot implementation guidance and milestone acceptance criteria.
options: Raw arcade — ultra-minimal forms and almost no decorative treatment.
Refined geometry — deliberate proportions, consistent edges, subtle shadows and excellent timing.
Showpiece — more elaborate luminous layers, visual embellishment, intense effects.
B with some C spectacle for key moments — unchosen option.
questions.rationale: Choose deliberate visual craftsmanship over decorative complexity. First perfect the readable machine made from a handful of shapes.
